tasks.question: What has to happen to a node before a kernel upgrade?

attempts.text: Before a kernel upgrade, nodes must be drained without exception. This means the node is cordoned first so the scheduler stops placing new pods on it, then the running pods are evicted and wait for them to reschedule elsewhere. This is necessary because an in-place kernel upgrade on a node that is still serving traffic has caused two of the three longest outages. After the packages are installed, the node must be rebooted to ensure the new kernel version is actually running, as a kernel installed but not booted causes audit discrepancies [1][3].

citations.title: Node maintenance
citations.quote:
## Kernel upgrades

Nodes are drained before any kernel upgrade, without exception. An in-place kernel
upgrade on a node that is still serving traffic has caused two of our three
longest outages.

Reboot the node after the packages are installed. A kernel that is installed but
not booted reports the new version to the package manager and the old version to
the running system, which makes every subsequent audit wrong.

citations.title: Node maintenance
citations.quote:
## Draining a node

Cordon the node first so the scheduler stops placing new pods on it. Cordoning is
not eviction: pods already running keep running, and the node keeps serving
traffic until they are moved.

Once the node is cordoned, evict the running pods and wait for them to reschedule
elsewhere. Eviction respects pod disruption budgets, so a workload that declares
one will be moved a replica at a time.

tasks.question: What happens to a webhook that cannot be delivered for a whole day?

attempts.text: A webhook delivery that cannot be delivered for a whole day is retried using exponential backoff with jitter, capped at twenty-four hours. After this period, the delivery is moved to a dead letter queue and the customer is notified by email [1].

citations.title: ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks
heading_path: ADR-0004: Use a message queue for outbound webhooks
citations.quote:
## Decision

Webhook deliveries are enqueued and delivered by a separate worker pool.

The queue is durable, so a delivery survives a deploy. Retries use exponential
backoff with jitter, capped at twenty-four hours, after which the delivery is
moved to a dead letter queue and the customer is notified by email.

tasks.question: What caused the checkout latency incident INC-2451?

attempts.text: The checkout latency incident INC-2451 was caused by connection pool exhaustion in the payments service. This exhaustion was triggered by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and held it for the duration of its run. A merchant onboarding campaign had increased the merchant count past the pool size for the first time, causing the job's connection usage to cross a threshold that had not been documented [2][5].

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency
citations.quote:
## Summary

Checkout p99 latency rose from 240 ms to 9 s for 47 minutes. No requests were
lost. The cause was connection pool exhaustion in the payments service, triggered
by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and
held it for the duration of its run.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-2451, checkout latency
citations.quote:
## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.

tasks.question: What is the per-service connection ceiling that RB-114 step three tells me to compare against?

attempts.text: The per-service connection ceiling that RB-114 step three tells you to compare against is 400 connections. This ceiling is enforced at the database by a role-level limit, so a service exceeding it has its connections refused rather than queued [2][4].

citations.title: RB-114: a saturated connection pool
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Read the pool utilisation for every replica, not the aggregate. An aggregate
   at 70 per cent hides one replica at 100.

2. Check whether the replica count changed in the last six hours. Each replica
   opens its own pool, so the connections a service asks for are the pool size
   multiplied by the replica count.

3. **Compare that product against the per-service connection ceiling.** The
   ceiling is a database setting and is listed in the service limits reference.
   If the product exceeds it, reduce the replica count until it does not. This is
   the step that resolves the common case, and it resolves it without a restart.

4. If the replica count did not change, look for a client holding connections
   open. Do not restart the service first: a restart clears the symptom and
   destroys the evidence, and the incident recurs on the next run of whatever was
   holding them.

citations.title: Service limits reference
citations.quote:
## Database connections

The per-service connection ceiling is **400**. It is enforced at the database by
a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused
rather than queued.

The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten
replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any
service using the default pool size.

Raising the ceiling requires the capacity review, because it is shared across
every service on the instance. The instance-wide maximum is 2000.

attempts.text: No, in INC-3187 the reconciliation job was not what saturated the pool. The per-service connection ceiling is enforced at the database, so nine replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the ceiling, causing the ninth replica's connections to be refused [1].

tasks.question: How many replicas can a payments service run on the default pool size before it hits the connection ceiling?

attempts.text: A payments service using the default pool size of 40 connections per replica can run up to nine replicas before it hits the per-service connection ceiling of 400. This is because the ceiling is reached at ten replicas (10 replicas × 40 connections = 400), and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any service using the default pool size [1].

citations.title: Service limits reference
citations.quote:
## Database connections

The per-service connection ceiling is **400**. It is enforced at the database by
a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused
rather than queued.

The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten
replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any
service using the default pool size.

Raising the ceiling requires the capacity review, because it is shared across
every service on the instance. The instance-wide maximum is 2000.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## What happened

The nightly reconciliation job was re-enabled after the capacity review signed it
off. It ran against the dedicated pool that INC-2451's actions created, and that
pool was correctly sized. The saturation was not the job.

A deployment three hours earlier had raised the payments service replica count
from four to nine. Each replica opens its own pool, and the per-service
connection ceiling is enforced at the database, not at the service — so nine
replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the ceiling and the
ninth replica's connections were refused.

citations.title: Postmortem: INC-3187, payments pool saturation
citations.quote:
## Actions

- The deployment pipeline now refuses a replica count that would exceed the
  ceiling. The current ceiling is recorded in the service limits reference, not
  in this document, for the reason given above.
- The 80 per cent pool utilisation alert now pages the primary on-call.
- RB-114 gained a fourth step covering replica-count changes.

tasks.question: A service is returning connection errors and I am about to restart it. Should I?

attempts.text: No, you should not restart the service first. According to the runbook RB-114, if the service is returning connection errors due to a saturated connection pool, you should first check for a client holding connections open. Restarting the service clears the symptom and destroys the evidence, and the incident will recur on the next run of whatever was holding the connections open [2].

citations.title: RB-114: a saturated connection pool
citations.quote:
## Steps

1. Read the pool utilisation for every replica, not the aggregate. An aggregate
   at 70 per cent hides one replica at 100.

2. Check whether the replica count changed in the last six hours. Each replica
   opens its own pool, so the connections a service asks for are the pool size
   multiplied by the replica count.

3. **Compare that product against the per-service connection ceiling.** The
   ceiling is a database setting and is listed in the service limits reference.
   If the product exceeds it, reduce the replica count until it does not. This is
   the step that resolves the common case, and it resolves it without a restart.

4. If the replica count did not change, look for a client holding connections
   open. Do not restart the service first: a restart clears the symptom and
   destroys the evidence, and the incident recurs on the next run of whatever was
   holding them.

tasks.question: Can I stop the connection errors by raising the pool size?

attempts.text: No, you should not raise the pool size to make the connection errors stop. The pool size ceiling is per service, so increasing the pool size per replica causes the service to reach the ceiling sooner, moving the failure from one replica to all of them at once [1]. Instead, you should compare the product of pool size and replica count against the per-service connection ceiling and reduce the replica count if it exceeds the ceiling [2]. Raising the ceiling itself requires a capacity review because it is shared with every other service on the database [1][6].

citations.title: RB-114: a saturated connection pool
citations.quote:
## What not to do

Do not raise the pool size to make the errors stop. The ceiling is per service,
so a larger pool per replica reaches it sooner, and the failure moves from one
replica to all of them at once.

Do not raise the ceiling without the capacity review. It is shared with every
other service on that database.

tasks.question: The deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine. Why nine specifically?

Therefore, the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine to avoid exceeding the ceiling [2].

citations.quote:

The per-service connection ceiling is **400**. It is enforced at the database by
a role-level limit, so a service that exceeds it has its connections refused
rather than queued.

The default pool size per replica is 40. The ceiling is therefore reached at ten
replicas, and the deployment pipeline refuses a replica count above nine for any
service using the default pool size.

Raising the ceiling requires the capacity review, because it is shared across
every service on the instance. The instance-wide maximum is 2000.

tasks.question: Both INC-2451 and INC-3187 exhausted a connection pool. What was different about the cause?

attempts.text:
Both INC-2451 and INC-3187 involved exhaustion of a connection pool in the payments service, but the causes differed:

- INC-2451 was caused by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and held it for the duration of its run. A merchant onboarding campaign had increased the merchant count past the pool size for the first time, causing the job's connection usage to cross a threshold that was not documented. The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident until this increase in merchants [5][6].

- INC-3187 was caused by a deployment that increased the payments service replica count from four to nine. Each replica opens its own pool, and the per-service connection ceiling is enforced at the database, not at the service. Therefore, nine replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the database connection ceiling, causing the ninth replica's connections to be refused. The nightly reconciliation job was not the cause in this incident [3][4].

In summary, INC-2451 was caused by a background job's connection usage exceeding the pool size due to increased merchants, while INC-3187 was caused by an increase in service replicas leading to exceeding the database connection ceiling [3][4][5][6].

by a background reconciliation job that opened one connection per merchant and
held it for the duration of its run.

citations.quote:
## What went wrong

The reconciliation job had run nightly for eight months without incident. A
merchant onboarding campaign had raised the merchant count past the pool size for
the first time, so the job's connection usage crossed a threshold nobody had
written down.

Restarting the service cleared the symptom but not the cause. Had the job been
scheduled to retry, the incident would have recurred within the hour.

citations.quote:

## What happened

The nightly reconciliation job was re-enabled after the capacity review signed it

from four to nine. Each replica opens its own pool, and the per-service
connection ceiling is enforced at the database, not at the service — so nine
replicas asking for their configured pool size exceeded the ceiling and the
ninth replica's connections were refused.
